# Opening: Christ had no human biological father

**Thesis.** The KJV presents Mary as the only human parent of Christ. His conception was "of the Holy Ghost." Joseph was his legal and supposed father, not his begetter. This is the standard reading, and I defend it as a chain, not as isolated verses.

## 1. The genealogy breaks its own pattern

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2-15 runs on one verb, "begat," from Abraham to Jacob. Then Matthew 1:16 reads: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** The verb in the pattern is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "he begat"), active, with a man as subject. In Matthew 1:16 the verb changes to ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born"), passive. The relative pronoun is ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"), feminine singular. It can refer only to Mary, not to Joseph, who is called ἄνδρα (andra, "husband, man") of Mary.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2-15 supplies the pattern. Matthew 1:16 departs from it exactly where Jesus is reached. Joseph is never said to have begotten him.

## 2. The source of the conception is stated

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The phrase is ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Holy Spirit"). ἐκ (ek, "out of") names source or origin. The participle is γεννηθέν (gennēthen, "that which is begotten or conceived"), the same root as the genealogy's verb. The text assigns the begetting to the Holy Ghost, not to Joseph.

**[L3]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." The verbs are ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai, "shall come upon") and ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "shall overshadow"). The phrase "therefore also" ties the title to this mode of conception. Matthew and Luke state the same fact independently.

## 3. Mary's virginity excludes a human father

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Matthew 1:18 places the conception "before they came together." Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** The verb in Luke 1:34 is γινώσκω (ginōskō, "to know"), used of marital relations. Matthew 1:25 has ἐγίνωσκεν ... ἕως οὗ (eginōsken ... heōs hou, "was knowing ... until which"), so the birth took place while she was a virgin. For Isaiah 7:14, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive," the Hebrew is עַלְמָה (ʿalmāh, "young woman of marriageable age, maiden"). Matthew 1:23 renders it παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin").

**[L3]** The KJV renders the same Hebrew word "virgin" in Genesis 24:43, of Rebekah, whom Genesis 24:16 describes as "a virgin, neither had any man known her." Matthew 1:23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled in this birth. Genesis 3:15 speaks of "her seed," the woman's seed, with no male named.

## 4. Joseph's fatherhood is only supposed

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." In Matthew 1:19 Joseph, on learning of the pregnancy, "was minded to put her away privily." He knew the child was not his.

**[L2]** ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed, reckoned") marks opinion or legal reckoning, not fact. Without the parenthesis the verse would have said ὤν (ōn, "being") alone.

**[L3]** The objections come from people who spoke from appearance. John 6:42 says, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Luke 2:48, "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing," is Mary's household usage. Christ answers in Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" That corrects the question of whose son he is. Galatians 4:4 says "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." The Greek γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "coming to be out of a woman") names the woman alone. Hebrews 10:5 says "a body hast thou prepared me," from κατηρτίσω (katartisō, "fitted, prepared").

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" pattern of Matthew 1:2-15: the active ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat") gives way to the passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born") with feminine ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"). Joseph is therefore not credited with begetting Jesus. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16; [L2] the verb and pronoun forms; [L3] the pattern of Matthew 1:2-15.
2. The text names the Holy Ghost as the source of the conception: ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Holy Spirit") in Matthew 1:18,20, confirmed by "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee" in Luke 1:35. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18,20; [L2] ἐκ and γεννηθέν; [L3] Luke 1:35.
3. Mary was a virgin at conception, so no human male was involved: Luke 1:34 "I know not a man" and Matthew 1:25 "knew her not till she had brought forth." Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34, Matthew 1:25; [L2] ἐγίνωσκεν (eginōsken, "was knowing") and παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin"); [L3] Isaiah 7:14 with Genesis 24:16,43 on עַלְמָה (ʿalmāh, "young woman, maiden").
4. Joseph's fatherhood is legal and reputed only: Luke 3:23 "as was supposed," with ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed"). Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23, Matthew 1:19; [L2] ἐνομίζετο; [L3] Luke 2:48-49, John 6:42, Galatians 4:4.
5. Christ had no human biological father. His human parentage is Mary alone, and his conception was of the Holy Ghost. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16,18,20, Luke 1:34-35; [L2] ἐξ ἧς, ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "coming to be out of a woman"); [L3] Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23, Galatians 4:4, Hebrews 10:5.

# Defender, Round 2: The Seed of David Reaches the Child Through Mary and Joseph's Legal Reception, Not Joseph's Begetting

The challenger's keystone is C5, "Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins." It rests on a premise the text never states, that the flesh from David's seed needs Joseph as begetter. I answer that first, then re-seat each pressed term in its chain (DD-1).

---

## A. The seed rows and the challenger's question

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
**[L2]** The verb is γενομένου (genomenou, "having come to be"), from γίνομαι (ginomai, "to become, come to be"), with ἐκ σπέρματος (ek spermatos, "out of seed"). It names a source of descent. It does not name a begetter.

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman."
**[L2]** The verb is the same, γενόμενον (genomenon, "having come to be"), with ἐκ (ek, "out of") and γυναικός (gynaikos, "woman").
**[L4]** Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4 use one verb with two sources, "seed of David" and "woman." Neither verse names a man as begetter. Read together, the woman is the one of David's seed. That chain rests on [L1] Romans 1:3, [L1] Galatians 4:4 and [L2] the shared verb.

**[L1]** Romans 9:5: "of whom as concerning the flesh Christ [came]."
**[L2]** This is the same phrase κατὰ σάρκα (kata sarka, "according to the flesh"). Here it is applied to descent from Israel as a people.
**[L4]** κατὰ σάρκα is therefore the language of ancestry. It does not require a named male begetter. This rests on [L1] Romans 9:5 and [L2] the identical phrase.

**Loins are ancestral.**
**[L1]** Hebrews 7:5: Levites "come out of the loins of Abraham." Hebrews 7:10: Levi "was yet in the loins of his father."
**[L3]** Genesis 35:11: "kings shall come out of thy loins."
**[L2]** The word is ὀσφύς (osphys, "loins"). Hebrews 7:5 uses it of Levites centuries after Abraham, through intervening fathers.
**[L4]** Acts 2:30, "of the fruit of his loins," therefore requires descent from David. It does not require Joseph as the last link. The footing is [L1] Hebrews 7:5,10, [L2] ὀσφύς, and [L3] Genesis 35:11.

**Where the Davidic line comes from, since the challenger says I offer none.**

1. **[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph." Luke 3:23: "which was [the son] of Heli." Joseph cannot have two begetting fathers.
2. **[L2]** In Luke 3:23 the KJV brackets "the son," marking it as supplied. The Greek has only the genitive τοῦ Ἡλί (tou Hēli, "of Heli"), a bare relation. Luke's line also stands under the parenthesis "as was supposed."
3. **[L3]** Ezra 2:61, the challenger's own verse, shows a man who "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai... and was called after their name." A man reckoned by his wife's father is a pattern the text itself records.
4. **[L1]** Luke 3:31: "which was [the son] of Nathan, which was [the son] of David." **[L3]** 2 Samuel 5:14 lists "Nathan, and Solomon" as sons of David.
5. **[L4]** Matthew's line runs through Solomon (Matthew 1:6). Luke's runs through Nathan. The two lines come from different sons of David, so Luke's cannot be Joseph's begetting line. It is the line of Mary through Heli. The footing is [L1] Matthew 1:16 and Luke 3:23, [L2] the bare genitive, and [L3] Ezra 2:61 and 2 Samuel 5:14.

**Matthew's line through Joseph also carries a bar to a begotten son.**
**[L1]** Matthew 1:12: "Jechonias begat Salathiel." **[L1]** Jeremiah 22:28 names "this man Coniah," and Jeremiah 22:30 says of him: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David."
**[L1]** Luke 1:32: the child receives "the throne of his father David."
**[L2]** "Coniah" and "Jechonias" are two forms of one name.
**[L4]** A son begotten by Joseph would be of Jechonias's seed, which is barred from David's throne. The child is promised that throne, so he is not Joseph's begotten seed. This rests on [L1] Matthew 1:12, [L1] Jeremiah 22:30, and [L1] Luke 1:32.

**Joseph's legal reception, the second channel.**
**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife." **[L1]** Matthew 1:21: "thou shalt call his name JESUS." **[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "he called his name JESUS." **[L1]** Luke 2:5: "To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife."
**[L3]** The law records a name carried legally apart from begetting. Deuteronomy 25:6: "the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother."
**[L4]** The Davidic son addressed in Matthew 1:20 is told to receive the child and name him. That gives the child the name and legal title of David's house. This rests on [L1] Matthew 1:20-21,25 and [L3] Deuteronomy 25:6.

**Answer to the challenger's question on Hebrews 7:14.**
**[L1]** Hebrews 7:14: "it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."
**[L2]** The verb is ἀνατέταλκεν (anatetalken, "has risen up, arisen"), which names an arising and not a begetter.
It is evident because Mary's line runs through Heli to Nathan and David (Luke 3:23,31). Joseph's legal line runs through Solomon (Matthew 1:6), and the house of David registered him with Mary (Luke 2:4-5).
**[L3]** Numbers 1:2 is a muster, "every male by their polls." It counts males for war and does not rule out a legal or maternal channel.

---

## B. Link by link

### D2: "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (margin: "Gr. begotten").
**[L2]** The participle is γεννηθέν (gennēthen, "that which is begotten"), with ἐν αὐτῇ (en autē, "in her"). The begetting is placed inside her body, as a womb event.
**[L3]** John 1:13 and 1 John 5:1 speak of believers' new birth, a later event. John 3:6 separates the two: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." Believers have a flesh-birth from a father and then a Spirit-birth. Matthew 1:20 has only the Spirit as begetter of what is in her, so the constructions are not parallel.

**Luke 1:35.**
**[L2]** ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai, "shall come upon") in Acts 1:8 is followed by power for witness. In Luke 1:35 the same verb is followed by "that holy thing which shall be born of thee," with "therefore also" (διὸ καί, dio kai, "for which reason also"). The verb takes its meaning from what follows it, and here that is a birth.
**[L1]** Luke 1:35, "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God," ties the title to the coming of the Holy Ghost.
**[L3]** 1 Chronicles 28:6 gives Solomon a covenant sonship, "I will be his father." It carries no "therefore" tied to a conception by the Spirit.

### D3: "a virgin at conception, so no human male"

**[L1]** Luke 1:31 promises: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son." Luke 1:34 asks: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
**[L2]** The Greek ἐπεὶ (epei, "since, seeing that") makes her state the reason for the question. A betrothed woman about to be taken in marriage would have no such question if the answer were her husband.
**[L1]** The angel's answer in Luke 1:35 is "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee." It names no husband.
**[L4]** The chain runs from [L1] Luke 1:31, 34-35 and [L2] ἐπεί to the conclusion that the angel's answer to "how" excludes Joseph.

**Matthew 1:18-20.**
**[L1]** Matthew 1:18 says she "was found with child" before "they came together." Matthew 1:19 says Joseph "was minded to put her away privily." Matthew 1:20 says "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
**[L2]** The "for" is γάρ (gar, "for, because"). It gives the ground on which Joseph's fear is removed, and that ground is the Holy Ghost. If Joseph had known her, the angel would have said the child was his.
**[L3]** Deuteronomy 22:24 treats a betrothed woman with another man as the other man having "humbled his neighbour's wife." Joseph's intent to put her away rests on that law.
**[L4]** The challenger says Matthew 1:19 has no verb of knowing. It does not need one. A just man would not plan to put away the mother of his own child. Matthew 1:19-20, γάρ, and Deuteronomy 22:24 support the reading that Joseph knew the child was not his.

**The challenger's own reading of Matthew 1:25.** He bounds the abstinence to after the taking in Matthew 1:24. Matthew 1:18 puts the finding of her pregnancy before "they came together." On his reading the conception came within the espousal and before the taking, and Matthew 1:19-20 treats it as Mary's trouble and not Joseph's.

**Isaiah 7:14.**
**[L1]** Isaiah 7:11 offers "a sign of the LORD thy God," and Isaiah 7:13 addresses "O house of David." **[L1]** Matthew 1:22 says "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled," and Matthew 1:23 quotes "Behold, a virgin shall be with child."
**[L2]** The word is παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin"). The challenger grants Matthew's application and says Luke uses the same word of Mary at Luke 1:27. Luke 1:27 states her state at betrothal, and Luke 1:34 and 1:35 state what followed.
**[L4]** A wife bearing her husband's son is no sign. The footing is [L1] Isaiah 7:11, [L1] Matthew 1:22-23, and [L2] παρθένος.

### D4: "as was supposed"

**[L2]** The challenger cites ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed") in Acts 16:13 ("wont"). In Luke's own writing, νομίζω (nomizō, "to suppose, reckon") in a supposition is of a belief later shown false.
**[L3]** Acts 14:19: Paul was drawn out "supposing he had been dead." Acts 21:29: "whom they supposed that Paul had brought into the temple."
**[L1]** In Luke 3:23, ὡς (hōs, "as") places the supposition apart from the fact.
**[L1]** Luke 2:43: "Joseph and his mother knew not." In Luke's own voice it is "Joseph and his mother," where a begotten son's parents would be "his father and mother."
**[L1]** Luke 2:48: "thy father and I." Luke 2:49: "my Father's business." Luke 2:50: "And they understood not the saying which he spake unto them." His reply answers the title and places it elsewhere.

### D1: Matthew 1:16

**[L2]** The challenger grants that ἐγεννήθη ἐξ ἧς (egennēthē ex hēs, "was born out of whom") names the mother. Matthew uses ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat") for every man in Matthew 1:2-15 and withholds it at the last step. A writer who had said "begat" fifteen times and wanted a begetter here would have said it again.
**[L3]** The "born of women" idiom in Matthew 11:11 and Job 14:1 is generic. Matthew 1:16 breaks a specific pattern at a specific point, and Matthew 1:18-20 explains the break.

---

## C. Reply to the unsupported-L4 list

1. **"He knew the child was not his."** Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:19-20, [L2] γάρ, [L3] Deuteronomy 22:24, as set out in B.
2. **"Mary alone."** Footing: [L1] Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4, [L2] the shared γίνομαι, [L1] Luke 3:23,31, [L3] Ezra 2:61 and 2 Samuel 5:14. Elisabeth is called "cousin" (Luke 1:36). The text does not say through which parent the kinship ran, so the relation does not decide Mary's tribe.
3. **"No human male."** Footing: [L1] Luke 1:31, 34-35 and [L2] ἐπεί, as set out in B.
4. **"The text assigns the begetting to the Holy Ghost."** Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:20, [L2] γεννηθέν with ἐν αὐτῇ, [L3] John 3:6, as set out in B.
5. **"Joseph is not credited with begetting."** Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:2-16, [L2] ἐγέννησεν against ἐγεννήθη, and [L1] Matthew 1:12 with Jeremiah 22:30 (the barred seed).

---

## CHAIN STATUS

The challenger's C1 through C4 are met in A and B. The seed of David comes through Mary by Luke's line and to Joseph's legal reception by Matthew's. Neither requires Joseph as begetter. C5 stands only on the unstated premise that David's flesh needs Joseph's loins, and the text supplies two lines of descent without it. Links 1 through 5 of my declared chain stand as declared.

- 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels."

- 1 Kings 8:19: "thy son that shall come forth out of thy loins."

**[L1] Hebrews 7:14**: "For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."

1. The promise requires flesh that proceeds out of a man's bowels and loins (2 Samuel 7:12; Acts 2:30).
2. The tribe is counted by the father's house (Numbers 1:2, 18).
3. Romans 1:3 says the promise was fulfilled "according to the flesh."
4. Therefore a man of David's house is the source of the child's flesh.

- Luke 2:4: "he was of the house and lineage of David."

- Luke 1:5: "his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elisabeth."

**[L3]** "Born of a woman" is the Bible's idiom for every mortal man, including men whose fathers are named:
- Matthew 11:11: "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist."
- Luke 1:13 names John's father: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son."
- Job 14:1: "Man that is born of a woman is of few days."

**[L4]** One passive verb that names the mother is never set against Romans 1:3, Acts 2:30 and Matthew 1:1, which name the father's line. It is the birth row, and it stands with them.

- 1 John 5:1: "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him."

- Matthew 1:19: "Joseph her husband."
- Matthew 1:20: "Mary thy wife."
- The law calls a betrothed damsel "his neighbour's wife" (Deuteronomy 22:24).

**[L4]** The chain therefore runs as follows:
1. The Bible's stated means of begetting is knowing: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1).
2. The seed must come out of a Davidic man's loins (Acts 2:30; Romans 1:3).

## 1. Held at L1–L2–L3 (no charge in either side's lists contests these)

- **Matthew 1:16's word forms.** The verb is passive (ἐγεννήθη, *egennēthē*) and the relative pronoun is feminine singular (ἐξ ἧς, *ex hēs*), against the active ἐγέννησεν (*egennēsen*) that governs Matthew 1:2–15. Neither side contests the forms; only the inference differs.
- **The Holy Ghost is the stated source of the conception.** Matthew 1:18, 20 (*ek pneumatos hagiou*), with the KJV margin at 1:20, "Gr. begotten." Both accept the wording.
- **Luke 1:34 is present tense.** "I know not a man" (*andra ou ginōskō*) states Mary's condition when the angel spoke (Luke 1:27, "a virgin espoused").
- **Joseph's Davidic house is stated.** Luke 2:4, "of the house and lineage of David"; Matthew 1:20, "Joseph, thou son of David." Both accept.
- **Joseph is named father by Mary, the narrator and the town:** Luke 2:48; Luke 2:27, 33; John 6:42. Both accept the naming.
- **Romans 1:3 names Christ's flesh as David's seed:** *ek spermatos Dauid kata sarka*. Both accept what the verse says; its sourcing is under 2.
- **ὀσφύς ("loins") is the procreative-body word:** Hebrews 7:5, 7:10; Genesis 35:11. Both accept.
- **Genesis 4:1 is the canon's stated means of begetting:** "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived" (also Deuteronomy 22:24's "his neighbour's wife," the betrothed damsel as wife).
- **Matthew 1:25's "till" bounds the abstinence.** Both accept the boundary.
- **The Davidic covenant sonship title is given to a begotten son:** Luke 1:32 with 1 Chronicles 28:6, "Solomon thy son... I have chosen him [to be] my son." Both treat this as covenant title, distinct from begetting.
